```{r llm-track-correspondance-between-experiments-in-paper-and-in-the-log-files-copied, eval = !isTRUE(get0("PARENT_RMD_EXISTS"))}

dat.moral.numbers.exp.correspondance <- list(
    # Basic experiment
    list(
        experimentID.data = "1", 
        experimentID.paper = "1a"
    ),
    # Replication with the conditions related to small number processing and the first item removed
    list(
        experimentID.data = "1b", 
        experimentID.paper = "1b"
    ),
    # 2a and 2b are switched
    # Ratio vs. victims
    list(
        experimentID.data = "2b", 
        experimentID.paper = "3a"
    ),
    # list(
    #     experimentID.data = "2a", 
    #     experimentID.paper = "2b"
    # ),
    # list(
    #     experimentID.data = "2c", 
    #     experimentID.paper = "2c"
    # ),
    # Ratio vs. utility
    # -   Exp 2a and 2c are replications of one another.
    # -   Exp 2d: Smaller differences in the number of victims
    # -   Exp 2b: Vs victims
    # -   Order in paper (2b => 2a), (2a,c,d = > 2bcd)
    list(
        experimentID.data = "2a", 
        experimentID.paper = "3b.1"
    ),
    list(
        experimentID.data = "2c", 
        experimentID.paper = "3b.2"
    ),
    # This is the combined experiment
    list(
        experimentID.data = "2ac", 
        experimentID.paper = "3b"
    ),
    list(
        experimentID.data = "2d", 
        experimentID.paper = "3c"
    ),
    # Moral vs. economic choices
    list(
        experimentID.data = "4", 
        experimentID.paper = "2"
    ),
    # Failed attempts to make the victims salient: 5 - 7
    # list(
    #     experimentID.data = "5", 
    #     experimentID.paper = "-1"
    # ),
    # list(
    #     experimentID.data = "6", 
    #     experimentID.paper = "-2"
    # ),
    # list(
    #     experimentID.data = "7", 
    #     experimentID.paper = "-3"
    # ),
    # Succesful attempt to make victims salient
    list(
        experimentID.data = "8", 
        experimentID.paper = "4"
    ),
    # Search for asymptote
    # list(
    #     experimentID.data = "9a", 
    #     experimentID.paper = "for SI"
    # ),
    list(
        experimentID.data = "9a", 
        experimentID.paper = "AS" # AS = asymptote search
    ),
    # Succesful attempt to make victims salient with higher ratios
    list(
        experimentID.data = "10", 
        experimentID.paper = "5"
    ),
    # Replication of experiment 10
    list(
        experimentID.data = "11",
        experimentID.paper = "6"
    ),
    # Combined vivacity experiments (8 + 10, 10 + 11)
    list(
        experimentID.data = "8+10",
        experimentID.paper = "4+5"
    ),
    list(
        experimentID.data = "10+11",
        experimentID.paper = "5+6"
    )
) %>%
    tibble::enframe(name = NULL, value = "data") %>%
    tidyr::unnest_wider(data) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), ~ stringr::str_c("exp", .x)))


```

dat.scenario.content <- dat.scenario.files %>% 
    dplyr::group_by(experimentID, condition) %>% 
    dplyr::group_modify(~  .x$file %>% 
                            xml2::read_xml(.) %>% 
                            XML::xmlParse() %>% 
                            XML::xmlToDataFrame()) %>% 
    dplyr::ungroup() %>% 
    tidyr::separate_wider_delim(label, names = c("label", "condition2"), delim = ".", too_few =  "align_start") %>% 
dplyr::mutate(condition = coalesce(condition, condition2)) %>% 
    dplyr::select(experimentID, condition, title, text, dplyr::starts_with("question"), dplyr::starts_with("option")) %>%
    dplyr::select(-dplyr::matches("anchor")) %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(question.acceptability = dplyr::coalesce(question, question.acceptability)) %>% 
    dplyr::select(-question) %>% 
    dplyr::rename(question.severity = question.severity.text) %>% 
    tidyr::drop_na(title, text) %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), ~ .x %>%
                            #stringr::str_remove_all("\\n") %>%
                             stringr::str_remove_all("[\\t\\n]") %>%
                             stringr::str_remove_all("\\[br\\]") %>%
                             stringr::str_squish()))

    # LOOP through the files using pmap_dfr
    purrr::pmap_dfr(\(relative_path, experimentID, experimentDesc, Group, rename_victims) {
        
        file_path <- here::here(EXPERIMENT_DIR, relative_path)
        
        df <- readr::read_csv(file_path, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(
                experimentID = experimentID,
                experimentDesc = experimentDesc,
                .before = 1
            )
        
        if(rlang::has_name(df, "ratio_saved_victims"))
            df <- dplyr::mutate(df, ratio_saved_victims = as.character(ratio_saved_victims))
        
        if (!is.na(Group)) {
            df <- dplyr::mutate(df, Group = Group, .before = 1)
        }
        
        if (rename_victims) {
            df <- dplyr::rename_with(df, ~ stringr::str_remove(.x, "1$"), dplyr::ends_with("1"))
        }
        
        return(df)
    }

```{r define-parameters-llm}


# Load API keys from .Renviron (not .profile)
list("OPENAI_API_KEY",
     "GEMINI_API_KEY",
     "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY",
     "DEEPSEEK_API_KEY",
     "MISTRAL_API_KEY",
     "QWEN_API_KEY"
     ) %>% 
    purrr::walk(~ assign(.x, Sys.getenv(.x), envir = .GlobalEnv))

# Secondary tier for experiments.ade@gmail.com, still at free tier
#@GEMINI_API_KEY <- Sys.getenv("GEMINI_API_KEY_SECONDARY")


# System prompts
SYSTEM_PROMPTS <- list(
    estimation = "When asked about the acceptability of an action, respond on a 6-point scale (1 = completely unacceptable, 6 = completely acceptable).",
    comparison = "When asked about the relative acceptability of two actions, respond on a 6-point scale (1 = Option 1 is much more unacceptable, 6 = Option 2 is much more acceptable)."
) %>% 
    purrr::map(~ glue("You are an average adult with no formal training in philosophy, ethics, or law. Your sense of right and wrong comes from everyday life—social norms, gut feelings, personal experience. You don’t try to be logically consistent or follow abstract moral rules. You react like a regular person would: practically, emotionally, and socially. You speak plainly, without academic or philosophical jargon. You can hesitate, contradict yourself, or be unsure—just like people often are. Please give your gut-level reaction, even if you’re not sure. 
      
     {.x}
      
    Respond **only** with a single digit (1–6). Do **not** add words, punctuation, or explanations. Any other output but the number will make your response unusable."))



# For gemini, the system prompt is part of the API call, not the message
SYSTEM_INSTRUCTIONS <- SYSTEM_PROMPTS %>% 
    purrr::map(~ list(
        parts = list(
            list(text = .x)
        )
    )
    )

LLM_OPTIONS <- list(
    max_attempts = 10,
    max_output_tokens = 10, # max tokens to generate in response
    temperature = .1, # controls randomness (0 = deterministic)
    top_k = 40,
    top_p = 1,
    # openAI specific options 
    n = 1, # number of completions
    # Number between -2.0 and 2.0. Positive values penalize new tokens based on their existing frequency in the text so far, decreasing the model's likelihood to repeat the same line verbatim.
    frequency_penalty = 0,  # optional, penalizes frequent tokens
    # Number between -2.0 and 2.0. Positive values penalize new tokens based on whether they appear in the text so far, increasing the model's likelihood to talk about new topics.
    presence_penalty = 0,    # optional, penalizes new topic introduction
    # ollama specific options
    num_ctx = 8192  # 8k context window
)

LLMS <- list(
    cloud = c(
        "gpt-4o-mini", # This seems to be completely deontological
        #"gpt-4o",
        #"gpt-4.1", # Not tests
        "gpt-4.1-mini",
        "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
        "gemini-2.5-flash",
        # "gemini-2.5-pro",
        "mistral-medium-latest",
        "deepseek-chat",
        "qwen-plus",
        "gpt-5-mini"
        ),
    local = c("llama3.2",
              "mistral",
              "mistral-nemo")
)

# Note about reasoning effort

    "cloud", "gpt-5-mini", "GPT-5 mini", "high",

    "cloud", "gemini-2.5-flash", "Gemini 2.5 flash", NA_character_,
#    "cloud", "gemini-2.5-pro", "Gemini 2.5 pro", NA_character_,
    "cloud", "mistral-medium-latest", "Mistral Medium", NA_character_,
    "cloud", "deepseek-chat", "Deepseek", NA_character_,

    "local", "mistral-nemo", "Mistral nemo (12.2B)", NA_character_,

) %>%

        )

LLM_LABELS <- LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE %>% 
    dplyr::select(-reasoning_effort, -model_type) %>%

LLM_URLS <- c(
    gpt = "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",

    `gemini-2.5-flash` = "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-flash:generateContent",
    `gemini-2.5-pro` = "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-pro:generateContent",
    ollama = "http://localhost:11434/api/chat",
    `mistral` = "https://api.mistral.ai/v1/chat/completions",

    `qwen-plus` = "https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1/chat/completions"

# Due to our latin square design, we already have 12 (10 for exp 4) subjects
# We multiple this by the number below. for example, with N_SUBJ_LLM_AFTER_LSD = 10, we effectively have 120 or 100 subjects
N_SUBJ_LLM_AFTER_LSD <- 10


RECALCULATE_LLM <- list(local = FALSE,
                        cloud = FALSE)

CHECKPOINT_DIR <- "checkpoints"

# Experiment 3 (exp2b, exp2ac) was rerun in moral_numbers_LLMs_exp3_rerun.Rmd because of a faulty comparison
# prompt. It is neither simulated nor loaded from the original result files here; its data are added from the
# rerun in exp3-rerun-add-data.
EXP3_IDS <- c("exp2b", "exp2ac")

drop_exp3_llm_data <- function(dat = ., source) {
    n_exp3 <- sum(dat$experimentID %in% EXP3_IDS)
    if (n_exp3 > 0) {
        warning(glue::glue("Removed {n_exp3} rows of the original Experiment 3 simulations from {source}; ",
                           "the Experiment 3 data come from the rerun."),
                call. = FALSE)
    }
    dat %>%
        dplyr::filter(!experimentID %in% EXP3_IDS)
}

    c("exp2b", "exp2ac", "exp4", "exp11"),
    combine_scenarios_and_number_conds
) %>%
    # Experiment 3 (exp2b, exp2ac) is simulated only in moral_numbers_LLMs_exp3_rerun.Rmd
    purrr::discard(\(dat) any(purrr::map_chr(dat$scenarios, ~ unique(.x$experimentID)) %in% EXP3_IDS))


dat_scenarios_numbers <- purrr::map(

                    ~ apply_latin_design(..1, ..2, dat_lsd = l_lsd)) %>% 
            purrr::set_names(combo_names)
    }
)


dat_scenarios_numbers_flat <- dat_scenarios_numbers %>%

## Methods 
We compared the responses of humans to those of several frontier (i.e., state-of-the-art) large language models (LLMs). We focused on three experiments: In Experiment 2, we asked whether LLMs are sensitive to the *beneficiary:victim* Weber ratio in moral and economic scenarios. In Experiment 3, we directly pitted Weber ratios against harm (the number of victims in Experiment 3a) and utility (the net number of survivors in Experiment 3b). Finally, in Experiment 6, we tested how LLMs react to manipulations of the vividness of the victims' deaths.

### Models and parameters

```{r exp3-rerun-methods-metadata}
# The Methods describe the Experiment 3 rerun (moral_numbers_LLMs_exp3_rerun.Rmd); its data are added in
# exp3-rerun-add-data
exp3_rerun_metadata_file <- here::here(OUTPUT_DIR, "llm_exp3_fixed_prompt.metadata.RData")
if (!file.exists(exp3_rerun_metadata_file)) {
    stop("Metadata of the Experiment 3 rerun not found: ", exp3_rerun_metadata_file)
}
load(exp3_rerun_metadata_file)

# Experiment 3 was simulated with the corrected comparison prompt of the rerun
SYSTEM_PROMPTS$comparison <- llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$system_prompts$comparison

# Option only used in the rerun (models with reasoning switched on)
LLM_OPTIONS$max_output_tokens_reasoning <- llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$llm_options$max_output_tokens_reasoning

# Cloud models of the rerun, with their reasoning efforts, for the text
llm_exp3_rerun_models_text <- llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$labels %>%
    dplyr::filter(model_type == "cloud") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(label = stringr::str_remove(label, " \\([^)]*reasoning\\)$")) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(label) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(
        text = dplyr::if_else(all(is.na(reasoning_effort)),
                              dplyr::first(label),
                              stringr::str_c(dplyr::first(label), " (reasoning effort ",
                                             knitr::combine_words(reasoning_effort), ")")),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::pull(text)
```

In Experiments 2 and 6, we tested `r combine_words(split(LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE, LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE$model_type)$cloud$label)`. We chose these models because they reflect a range of jurisdictions (China, France and USA) and thus potentially differences in training corpora and alignment procedures (i.e., post-training procedures used to shape model behavior according to values determined by the model creators and their jurisdictions). We used different versions of OpenAI's GPT models because, during initial non-systematic exploration, some models seemed more deontological than others, and because this allowed us to set the reasoning effort parameter in GPT-5 mini. (This parameter controls how many internal and intermediate reasoning steps the model generates before producing its final response.) We also explored several smaller models run on a local computer through ollama (https://ollama.com/), namely `r combine_words(split(LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE, LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE$model_type)$local$label)`.

Experiment 3 was simulated separately. In our initial simulations of Experiment 3, the system prompt describing the response scale contained an error (both ends of the scale favored Option 2), and we thus reran these simulations with a corrected prompt (see Table \ref{tab:LLM-system-prompt-print}). As some of the models used in Experiments 2 and 6 had been retired by then, we used the current mid-tier models of the same providers, namely `r combine_words(llm_exp3_rerun_models_text)`, as well as the same local models. In these simulations, we also corrected the wording error in the economic version of the *Aqueduct in the desert* scenario (see SI \ref{app:scenario-errors-exp3}), which human participants had seen in its erroneous form. Further, inspection of preliminary simulations suggested that some models might have confused the response scale (1--6) with the option labels (1 vs. 2). To avoid such confusions, we switched the option labels to A vs. B. Finally, as in the human experiments, we counterbalanced the order of the two options across simulated participants, such that half of them saw the high-ratio option as Option A and half of them as Option B (in our initial simulations, it was always presented first).

For models that support these options, we used the parameters given in Table \ref{tab:LLM-option-print} or their equivalents. The system prompts (general instructions on how the model should respond, passed to the model prior to the experimental trials) are given in Table \ref{tab:LLM-system-prompt-print}.

### Procedure

We kept the procedure as closely as possible to the human experiments, where participants rated multiple scenarios in each experiment. We achieved this by treating trials as an ongoing, incremental conversation. On the first trial, the API calls contained the system prompt as well as the first scenario. On the second trial, they contained the system prompt, the first scenario together with the model's answer on the first trial (provided as a message from the *assistant* role or the equivalent in other models), as well as the second scenario. Finally, on the last trial, the API calls contained the system prompt, all previous scenarios together with the model's answers, as well as the last scenario. The main procedural difference to the human experiments is thus that all contrasts (e.g., moral vs. economic in Experiments 2 and 3; vivid vs. neutral in Experiment 6) are treated as between-participant contrasts rather than within-participant contrasts as the latter would not be meaningful in models.

```{r number-of-trials-print}

# Design of all experiments: Experiments 2 and 6 from this file, Experiment 3 from the rerun
dat_llm_design <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    dat_scenarios_numbers_flat %>%
        dplyr::select(experimentID, condition, Group, lsd_order, subj),
    llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$design %>%
        dplyr::select(experimentID, condition, ratioOrder, Group, lsd_order, subj) 
) 

dat_llm_n_trials_responses <- purrr::reduce(
    list(

        # Cells in latin square (in the Experiment 3 rerun, one Latin square per option order)
        dat_llm_design %>%
            dplyr::distinct(experimentID, condition, Group, ratioOrder, lsd_order)  %>%
            dplyr::count(experimentID, condition, Group, ratioOrder)  %>% 
            dplyr::rename("Number of cells" = n),
        
        # Number of trial per subject
        dat_llm_design %>%
            dplyr::count(experimentID, condition, Group, ratioOrder, subj)  %>% 
            dplyr::distinct(experimentID, condition, Group, ratioOrder, n) %>% 
            dplyr::rename("Number of trials/participant" = n),
        
        # Number of Responses
        dat_llm_design %>%
            dplyr::count(experimentID, condition, Group, ratioOrder) %>%
            dplyr::rename("Number of responses" = n),

        # Number of participants (counted, as the number of replicates per cell differs between the original
        # simulations and the Experiment 3 rerun)
        dat_llm_design %>%
            dplyr::distinct(experimentID, condition, Group, ratioOrder, subj) %>%
            dplyr::count(experimentID, condition, Group, ratioOrder) %>%
            dplyr::rename("Number of participants" = n)
    ),
    ~ dplyr::left_join(
        .x, 
        .y, 
        by = c("experimentID", "condition", "Group", "ratioOrder")
    )   
) %>% 
    dplyr::relocate("Number of participants", .after = `Number of cells`)

# Experiment 3 rerun (rows with an option order): simulated participants per Latin square cell, for the text
n_subj_per_cell_llm_exp3 <- dat_llm_n_trials_responses %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(ratioOrder)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(n = `Number of participants` / `Number of cells`) %>%
    dplyr::pull(n) %>%
    unique()

stopifnot(length(n_subj_per_cell_llm_exp3) == 1)

dat_llm_n_trials_responses %>%
    format_exp_info() %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        ratioOrder = dplyr::if_else(
            stringr::str_detect(ratioOrder, "first"),
            "High-ratio option first",
            "High-ratio option second"
        ),
        condition = relabel_conds_llm(condition),
        Group = dplyr::coalesce(Group, ratioOrder)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(-ratioOrder) %>%
    dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_remove(.x, "Number of"),
                       dplyr::starts_with("Number of")) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(experimentID, condition, Group) %>% 
    dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_to_title(.x)) %>%
    kable.packed(
        "Experimentid", # Due to rename_width
        caption = paste0(
            "Experimental design summary for LLM simulations. Each cell in the Latin square design was tested with ",
            N_SUBJ_LLM_AFTER_LSD, " (Experiments 2 and 6) or ", n_subj_per_cell_llm_exp3,
            " (Experiment 3) independent response sets, with each response set treated as a simulated participant. The table shows the number of conditions (cells), simulated participants, trials per participant, and total responses for each experiment. In Experiment 3, \\emph{Group} refers to the order of the two options (high-ratio option presented first vs. second), with a separate Latin square for each order. In Experiment 6, \\emph{Group} refers to two different sets of victim and beneficiary numbers crossed with the neutral/vivid manipulation, resulting in four conditions total."
        ),
        #col.names = en_math_col_names(., 1),
        booktabs = TRUE,
        longtable = FALSE,
        escape = FALSE) %>%
    kableExtra::row_spec(0, bold = TRUE) %>%
    kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Number of" = 4), bold = TRUE) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped",
        "scale_down",
        "hold_position",
        "repeat_header")) %>% 
    kableExtra::kable_classic_2()
    

```


As in the human experiments, our simulations used a latin square design, spanned by the available scenarios in each cell and the number conditions (see SI \@ref(app:design)). In Experiment 6, and as in the human experiments, we used two counterbalanced sets of number conditions, involving different numbers of victims and beneficiaries. 

For each design cell in Experiments 2 and 6, we obtained `r N_SUBJ_LLM_AFTER_LSD` simulated participants (i.e., independent conversations with the models) for each model. In Experiment 3, the Latin square was additionally crossed with the order of the two options (high-ratio option presented first vs. second), and we obtained `r n_subj_per_cell_llm_exp3` sets of independent responses per cell. Overall, this resulted in the numbers of cells, (simulated) participants, trials per participant, and responses given in Table \ref{tab:number-of-trials-print}, with a total of `r format(sum(dat_llm_n_trials_responses[["Number of participants"]]), big.mark = ",")` simulated participants and `r format(sum(dat_llm_n_trials_responses[["Number of responses"]]), big.mark = ",")` responses.

```{r run-exp}




if(isTRUE(RECALCULATE_LLM$local)){

    # When run through Rscript, llama3.2 takes 684 s/11.4 min per subject (after application of the latin square design, so 10 or 12 subjects in total, depending on the experiment).
    # With 10 replicates of each cell (i.e., 100 or 120 subjects), this would take roughly 2h per model, and 4h for llama and mistral-nemo

    dat_llm_results_exps_local <- dat_scenarios_numbers_flat %>% 
        tidyr::expand_grid(model = LLMS$local) %>% 
        dplyr::group_by(model, experimentID, experimentDesc, condition, Group, lsd_order, combo_id, subj) %>% 
        dplyr::group_modify(~ get_api_response_wrapper_df(.x, .y, verbose = TRUE, DEBUG = FALSE),
                            .keep = FALSE) %>% 
        tidyr::unnest(response) %>% 
        dplyr::mutate(response = as.numeric(response)) %>% 
        dplyr::rename(rating.raw = response) %>% 
        dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_replace_all(.x, "_", "."), dplyr::matches("n_"))  %>%
        tidyr::drop_na(rating.raw) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(c("n.victims", "n.saved")), as.integer),
                      rating.bin = 1 * (rating.raw > 3),
                      n.net.saved =  n.saved - n.victims,
                      n.total = n.victims + n.saved)

    save(
        dat_llm_results_exps_local,
        file = here::here(
            OUTPUT_DIR,
            "llm_test.all_exps.local_models.RData"
            )
        )
} else {
    load(here::here(
        OUTPUT_DIR,
        "llm_test.all_exps.local_models.RData"
    )
    )
    dat_llm_results_exps_local <- drop_exp3_llm_data(dat_llm_results_exps_local, "llm_test.all_exps.local_models.RData")
}
 

if(isTRUE(RECALCULATE_LLM$cloud)){   
    
    # Parellelize only by model
    # We save model specific RData files from within the loop as well as a general RData file with some reformatting
    
    safe_get_api_response <- purrr::safely(get_api_response_wrapper_df, otherwise = NULL)
    
    dat_llm_results_exps_cloud <- furrr::future_map_dfr(
        LLMS$cloud,
        \(model){
            Sys.sleep(runif(1, 0.1, 0.5))  # jittered sleep
            
            partial_result <- dat_scenarios_numbers_flat %>% 
                dplyr::mutate(model = model) %>% 
                dplyr::group_by(model, experimentID, experimentDesc, condition, Group, lsd_order, combo_id, subj) %>% 
                dplyr::group_modify(
                    \(dat, dat_grp){
                        
                        res <- safe_get_api_response(dat, dat_grp, verbose = TRUE, DEBUG = FALSE)
                        
                        if (!is.null(res$error)) {
                            tibble::tibble(
                                model = dat_grp$model,
                                experimentID = dat_grp$experimentID,
                                error = paste("Error:", res$error$message)
                            )
                        } else {
                            res$result
                        }
                    },
                    .keep = FALSE)
            
            # Save model specific data file
            result_var_name <- glue::glue("dat_llm_results_exps_cloud_{gsub('-', '_', model)}")
            result_file_name <- glue::glue("llm_test.all_exps.{model}.RData")
            # Don't care if it's in the global environment or not as it will be saved anyhow
            assign(result_var_name,
                   partial_result, 
                   envir = .GlobalEnv)
            
            save(list = result_var_name,
                 file = here::here(
                     OUTPUT_DIR,
                     result_file_name
                 )
            )
            
            partial_result
        }
        
    ) %>% 
        tidyr::unnest(response, keep_empty = TRUE) %>% 
        dplyr::mutate(response = as.numeric(response)) %>% 
        dplyr::rename(rating.raw = response) %>% 
        dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_replace_all(.x, "_", "."), dplyr::matches("n_"))  %>%
        tidyr::drop_na(rating.raw) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(c("n.victims", "n.saved")), as.integer),
                      rating.bin = 1 * (rating.raw > 3),
                      n.net.saved =  n.saved - n.victims,
                      n.total = n.victims + n.saved)


    # save general data file
    # Commented out as we don't seem to use it anywhere    
        
    # save(
    #     dat_llm_results_exps_cloud, 
    #     file = paste0("output/", "llm_test.all_exps.cloud_models.RData"))
    
    
} else {
    
    
    # load general data file
    # Commented out as we don't seem to use it anywhere    
    # load(paste0("output/", "llm_test.all_exps.cloud_models.RData"))
    
    
    l_cloud_result_vars <- 
        purrr::map(
            LLMS$cloud,
            \(model){
                
                file_name <- glue::glue("llm_test.all_exps.{model}.RData")     
                
                file <- here::here(OUTPUT_DIR, file_name)
            
                if(!file.exists(file)) return(NA_character_)
            
                tmp_env <- new.env()
                load(file, envir = tmp_env)
                var_names_in_env <- ls(tmp_env) 
            
                purrr::walk(var_names_in_env,
                     ~ assign(.x, drop_exp3_llm_data(tmp_env[[.x]], file_name), envir = .GlobalEnv)
                )
                
            var_names_in_env
        }
    ) %>% 
        purrr::flatten_chr() %>% 
        purrr::discard(is.na)
    


        
}

exp3_rerun_metadata_file <- here::here(OUTPUT_DIR, "llm_exp3_fixed_prompt.metadata.RData")
if (!file.exists(exp3_rerun_metadata_file)) {
    stop("Metadata of the Experiment 3 rerun not found: ", exp3_rerun_metadata_file)
}
load(exp3_rerun_metadata_file)

exp3_rerun_files_missing <- c(llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$local_file, llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$cloud_runs$file) %>%
    purrr::discard(~ file.exists(here::here(OUTPUT_DIR, .x)))
if (length(exp3_rerun_files_missing) > 0) {
    stop("Result files of the Experiment 3 rerun not found in ", OUTPUT_DIR, ": ",
         paste(exp3_rerun_files_missing, collapse = ", "))
}

# In the analyses, models are identified by <model>-reasoning-<effort> (or <model> without reasoning effort).
# mistral-medium-latest pointed to Mistral Medium 3 in the original simulations and to Mistral Medium 3.5 in
# the rerun, so the rerun version gets its own name.
EXP3_RERUN_MODEL_RENAMES <- c(`mistral-medium-latest` = "mistral-medium-3.5")

make_llm_model_key <- function(model, reasoning_effort) {
    # !!! is rlang's splice operator. it unpacks the named list in three separate arguments	
    model <- dplyr::recode(model, !!!EXP3_RERUN_MODEL_RENAMES)
    dplyr::if_else(is.na(reasoning_effort),
                   model,
                   stringr::str_c(model, "-reasoning-", reasoning_effort))
}

# Each result file contains a single data frame
load_exp3_rerun_file <- function(file) {
    load_file_as_value(here::here(OUTPUT_DIR, file))
}

dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    # Local models (already processed in the rerun)
    load_exp3_rerun_file(llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$local_file),
    # Cloud models: one file per model and reasoning effort
    purrr::map(
        llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$cloud_runs$file,
        \(file) {
            dat <- load_exp3_rerun_file(file)
            # Failed conversations are recorded in the error column
            if ("error" %in% names(dat)) {
                dat <- dat %>%
                    dplyr::filter(is.na(error))
            }
            dat %>%
                dplyr::mutate(
                    response = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(response)),
                    # Answers that do not start with a rating, but end with a sentence followed by a rating
                    # (e.g., "... Gut says option B. 4"; mainly Claude Sonnet 5.5): the final rating is used
                    response = dplyr::if_else(
                        response %in% 1:6,
                        response,
                        suppressWarnings(as.numeric(stringr::str_match(response_raw, "\\.\\s*([1-6])\\s*$")[, 2]))
                    )
                ) %>%
                dplyr::rename(rating.raw = response) %>%
                dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_replace_all(.x, "_", "."), dplyr::matches("n_")) %>%
                dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(c("n.victims", "n.saved")), as.integer),
                              rating.bin = 1 * (rating.raw > 3),
                              n.net.saved = n.saved - n.victims,
                              n.total = n.victims + n.saved)
        }
    ) %>%
        purrr::list_rbind()
) 

# Extract responses with text in the response; this is a problem with claude 
dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun_text_responses <- dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(response_raw = stringr::str_squish(response_raw)) %>%
    dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(response_raw, "[^\\d]"))

# Now filter invalid responses
dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun <- dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun %>%
    # Valid responses are ratings from 1 to 6 (for local and cloud models alike)
    dplyr::filter(rating.raw %in% 1:6) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(model = make_llm_model_key(model, reasoning_effort)) %>%
    # For compatibility with the human experiments
    dplyr::rename(ResponseId = subj)

stopifnot(
    "The Experiment 3 rerun contains other experiments" =
        all(dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun$experimentID %in% EXP3_IDS)
)

dat_llm_results_exps <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    dat_llm_results_exps,
    dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun
)

# Add the rerun's cloud models (the local models are the same as in the original simulations)
LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE,
    llm_exp3_rerun_metadata$labels %>%
        dplyr::filter(model_type == "cloud") %>%
        dplyr::mutate(model = make_llm_model_key(model, reasoning_effort))
)

LLM_LABELS <- LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE %>%
    dplyr::select(-reasoning_effort, -model_type) %>%
    tibble::deframe()
```

```{r invert-rartings-exp2-llm}

# In the human experiments, 6 means the high ratio option is code as the second option (though the option order is counterbalanced, here it's the first)

# In the Experiment 3 rerun (added in exp3-rerun-add-data), the option order is counterbalanced (ratioOrder):
# ratings are inverted only when the high-ratio option was option 1; when it was option 2, 6 already means the
# high-ratio option. The original Experiment 3 simulations (high-ratio option always option 1, no ratioOrder) are
# not analyzed any more.
if (!"ratioOrder" %in% names(dat_llm_results_exps)) {
    stop("ratioOrder not found: the Experiment 3 data must come from the rerun (moral_numbers_LLMs_exp3_rerun.Rmd).")
}
if (any(stringr::str_detect(dat_llm_results_exps$experimentID, "exp2") & is.na(dat_llm_results_exps$ratioOrder))) {
    stop("Experiment 3 data without ratioOrder: the Experiment 3 data must come from the rerun (moral_numbers_LLMs_exp3_rerun.Rmd).")
}

dat_llm_results_exps <- dat_llm_results_exps %>%
    dplyr::mutate(invert = stringr::str_detect(experimentID, "exp2") & ratioOrder %in% "high_ratio_first",
                  rating.bin = dplyr::if_else(invert,
                                               1 - rating.bin, rating.bin),
                  rating.raw = dplyr::if_else(invert,
                                               7 - rating.raw, rating.raw)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(-invert)


```

```{r verify-llm-results}

```{r verify-llm-results-claude}
dat_llm_data_loss_claude <- dat_llm_results_exps %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(response_valid = is.finite(rating.bin) & is.finite(rating.raw)) %>% 
    dplyr::filter(
        response_valid,
        model != "participants",
        stringr::str_detect(experimentID, "exp2")
    ) %>%
    dplyr::count(experimentID, condition, model) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(experimentID, condition) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(n_expected = max(n)) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup() %>%
    dplyr::filter(
     stringr::str_detect(model, "claude")
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        p_data_loss = 100* (1 - n / n_expected),
        .keep = "unused"
    )

```

To validate the LLM results, we recorded the number of valid responses for each experiment and condition, where a valid response is a single digit between 1 and 6 with no additional words, punctuation, or explanations (defined by the system prompts shown in Table \ref{tab:LLM-system-prompt-print}). In Experiment 3, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (and, in a single trial, Gemini 3.8 Flash) often answered with a justification followed by a rating (e.g., "... Gut says option B. 4"); in these cases, we used the final rating if it followed the end of a sentence. As shown in Table \ref{tab:verify-llm-results}, when excluding Claude Sonnet 5.5, data loss was minimal (at most `r round(max_p_data_loss_without_claude, 1)`%). In Experiment 3b, Claude Sonnet 5.5 returned many undefined responses or responses with extraneous justifications beyond the requested numerical values, leading to loss of between `r knitr::combine_words(round(range(dat_llm_data_loss_claude %>% dplyr::filter(experimentID == "exp2ac") %>% dplyr::pull(p_data_loss)), 1))`% of the data. Further, when these text answers were fed back into the ongoing conversations, some later requests were blocked by a filter of the Anthropic API, which flagged them as attempts to reverse engineer or duplicate model outputs. As this pattern replicated across reasoning efforts, it appears that Claude Sonnet 5.5 has difficulties following instructions in Experiment 3b, but showed similarly low rates of data loss as did the other models in the other experiments, including Experiment 3a.

economic version of that scenario was corrected in the Experiment 3 rerun (moral_numbers_LLMs_exp3_rerun.Rmd). -->

dat_llm_human_acceptability <- dat.moral.numbers %>%

dat_llm_results_exps <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    dat_llm_results_exps,

    dplyr::bind_rows(
        # Experiments 2 and 3a (original and scenario-excluded versions)
        dat_llm_human_acceptability %>%
            select_exps(
                expID_clean = c("exp4", "exp2b"),
                require_single_version = FALSE
            ),
        # Experiment 3b: Experiments 2a and 2c are replications of one another, so we pool them
        dat_llm_human_acceptability %>%
            pool_exps(expID_clean = c("exp2a", "exp2c"), expID_pooled = "exp2ac"),
        # Experiment 6: participants for whom the vivacity manipulation was successful,
        # labelled exp11 like the LLM data
        dat_llm_human_acceptability %>%
            select_exps(
                expID_clean = "exp11",
                require_single_version = TRUE,
                vivacity_filtered = TRUE
            ) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(experimentID = "exp11")
    ) %>%
        # scenarioID: for the random effect of scenario in the order-effect models (LLM data: title)
        dplyr::select(experimentID, decisionType, vivacity, ResponseId, scenarioID,
                      dplyr::matches("^(n\\.|ratio|rating)"))  %>%
        # Make consistent with LLM format
        dplyr::mutate(n.saved = dplyr::coalesce(n.saved, n.saved1)) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(n.victims = dplyr::coalesce(n.victims, n.victims1)) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(n.total = dplyr::coalesce(n.total, n.total1)) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(ratio = dplyr::coalesce(ratio, ratio1)) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(n.net.saved = dplyr::coalesce(n.net.saved, n.net.saved1)) %>%
        # ratioOrder is kept (option order in Experiment 3, as in the LLM data)
        dplyr::select(-dplyr::ends_with("1"), -c(ratio.of.net.saved, ratio.theoretical, ratio.of.ratios)) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(condition = dplyr::coalesce(decisionType, vivacity)) %>% 
        dplyr::select(-decisionType, -vivacity) %>% 
        dplyr::mutate(model = "participants") 
)

```{r llm-make-fit}


dat_llm_fits_1_param <- dat_llm_results_exps_long %>% 
    dplyr::filter(measure == "bin",
                  experimentID %in% c("exp4", "exp11")) %>%

            start = FIT_PARAMS$start["w"],
            #nlsLM specific options

            lower = FIT_PARAMS$lower["w"],
            upper = FIT_PARAMS$upper["w"]) %>% 
            broom::tidy(),
        error = function(e) data.frame(
            term = c("w")) %>% 
            dplyr::mutate(
                estimate = NA,
                std.error = NA,
                statistic = NA,
                p.value = NA
            )

    dplyr::group_by(model, experimentID, condition) %>% 
    dplyr::group_modify(~ tryCatch(

            rating ~ acceptability.fnc (w, 
                                        n.saved, n.victims,
                                        a = a),
            data = .x,
            # This is a list
            start = FIT_PARAMS$start,
            #nlsLM specific options
            # These are vectors
            lower = FIT_PARAMS$lower,
            upper = FIT_PARAMS$upper) %>%  
            broom::tidy(),
        error = function(e) data.frame(
            term = c("w", "a")) %>%

                    estimate = NA,

## Results
In the simulations below, we asked whether the models reproduced the human pattern *qualitatively*, as we had no particular expectation that LLMs might provide a quantitative fit to human behavior. We were thus mainly concerned with the question of whether the models showed preferences in the same direction as humans, and whether these preferences were affected by the same factors.

### Experiment 2 


```{r plot-llm-results-prepare-single-option-responses}

)

#### Frontier models

```{r plot-llm-results-exp4-ratio-cloud, fig.height=14, fig.width=16, fig.cap="Acceptability of sacrificial decisions as a function of \\emph{beneficiary:victim} Weber ratios in Experiment 2 for \\emph{frontier models}. Points represent mean acceptability with 95% confidence intervals. Curves show psychophysical model fits for the average responses across simulated participants.  (a) \\emph{Binarized responses} (acceptable/unacceptable) for moral (top) and economic (bottom) scenarios. (b) \\emph{Raw} responses on a 6-point scale. Most models showed some sensitivity to Weber ratios in moral scenarios at least when considering raw ratings, though some models (GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-5 mini variants, Qwen-plus) were substantially more lenient than humans.", out.width="\\textwidth", out.extra="keepaspectratio"}

p_list_llm_single_option$cloud$exp4 %>% 
    purrr::map(\(x) purrr::pluck(x, "plot.by.ratio") + 
                   ggthemes::theme_clean(20))  %>% 
    rev %>% 
    ggpubr::ggarrange(
        plotlist = .,
        common.legend = TRUE,
        legend = "bottom",
        ncol = 1,
        nrow = 2,
        labels = "auto",
        font.label = list(size = 32) 
    ) 



```

In Experiment 2, we asked whether the models would be sensitive to the *beneficiary:victim* Weber ratio in moral and economic scenarios. The results for frontier models and the binarized ratings (responses transformed into acceptable/unacceptable decisions on which our model is based) are shown in Figure \ref{fig:plot-llm-results-exp4-ratio-cloud}a. For moral scenarios, most LLMs showed some sensitivity to Weber ratios, though the quality of fit to our psychophysical model varied. However, some models were much more likely to endorse a sacrificial decision than humans, namely GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-5 mini (with all reasoning effort settings) and Qwen-plus.

In contrast, for economic scenarios, Gemini-2.5 flash and GPT-5 mini (all reasoning effort settings) showed no sensitivity to Weber ratios when considering binarized responses. Nevertheless, Figure \ref{fig:plot-llm-results-exp4-ratio-cloud}b shows that, when considering the raw (rather than binarized) responses, these models also showed some limited sensitivity to Weber ratios.

            " " = 1,
            # Each of Human, Frontier Models, and Local Models gets 3 as a value
            purrr::set_names(
                rep(3, 3),
                names(dat_llm_fits_1_param_for_table)[-1] %>% 
                    stringr::str_remove("_.*$") %>% 
                    unique
            )
        ),
        bold = TRUE,
        align = "c"
    ) %>% 
    kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped",
        "scale_down",
        "hold_position",
        "repeat_header")) %>% 
    kableExtra::kable_classic_2()
    


```

Figure \ref{fig:plot-llm-results-exp4-ratio-cloud} also shows that ratings were substantially higher for economic scenarios than for moral scenarios, mirroring the pattern seen in human participants.

#### Local models


```{r plot-llm-results-exp4-ratio-local, fig.height=14, fig.width=16, fig.cap="Acceptability of sacrificial decisions as a function of \\emph{beneficiary:victim} Weber ratios in Experiment 2 for \\emph{local models}. Points represent mean acceptability with 95% confidence intervals. Curves show psychophysical model fits for the average responses across simulated participants. (a) \\emph{Binarized responses} (acceptable/unacceptable) for moral (top) and economic (bottom) scenarios. (b) \\emph{Raw} responses on a 6-point scale. Unlike frontier models, local models showed no discernible sensitivity to Weber ratios in either moral or economic scenarios. However, most models showed higher acceptability rates for economic than for moral decisions.", out.width="\\textwidth", out.extra="keepaspectratio"}

p_list_llm_single_option$local$exp4 %>% 
    purrr::map(\(x) purrr::pluck(x, "plot.by.ratio") + 
                   ggthemes::theme_clean(20)
               )  %>% 
    rev %>% 
    ggpubr::ggarrange(
        plotlist = .,

        legend = "bottom",
        ncol = 1,
        nrow = 2,

```



In contrast to the frontier models, the (smaller) local models showed no discernible sensitivity to Weber ratios, neither in binary ratings (see Figure \ref{fig:plot-llm-results-exp4-ratio-local}a) nor in raw ratings (see Figure \ref{fig:plot-llm-results-exp4-ratio-local}b). However, most did show higher acceptability rates for economic than for moral decisions.

```{r plot-llm-results-exp4-harm-utility-cloud-raw, fig.height=10, fig.width=14,fig.cap="Acceptability as a function of utility and harm for frontier models in Exp 2 (raw)", eval = FALSE}

p_list_llm_single_option$cloud$exp4$raw %>%
    purrr::discard_at("plot.by.ratio") %>%
    ggpubr::ggarrange(plotlist = .,
                      nrow = 2,
                      common.legend = FALSE)

```

Accordingly, and as shown in Table \ref{tab:print-fits-exp2}, when fitting the model behavior to our decision model, the noise parameter ($w$) was higher in the moral than in the economic condition for most models, with the exception of Llama 3.2 (3.2B), where the two values were comparable.

#### Summary

Taken together, these results suggest that LLMs can show some sensitivity to Weber ratios in both moral and economic decisions, at least for large frontier models, but not for smaller local models. Further, most models rated economic sacrifices as more acceptable than moral sacrifices. However, the fit to our psychophysical model was of variable quality. 


`r clearpage()`

### Experiment 3

In Experiment 3, participants had to choose between two options. In Experiment 3a, one option had a higher *beneficiary:victim* Weber ratio and a higher number of victims (i.e., harm), while the other had a lower *beneficiary:victim* Weber ratio and also lower harm. In Experiment 3b, we similarly pitted Weber ratios against utility. In moral situations, humans prefer to maximize Weber ratios over minimizing harm or maximizing utility. In economic situations, in contrast, they still prioritize Weber ratios over harm, but prioritize utility over Weber ratios. 

```{r llm-exp2-descriptives-calculate}


# By subject averages, keeping the option order (ratioOrder; between simulated participants and participants)
dat_llm_results_exp2_by_subject <- dat_llm_results_exps_long %>%
    select_exps(
        expID_clean = c("exp2ac", "exp2b"),
        require_single_version = FALSE
    ) %>%
    classify_models() %>%
    dplyr::group_by(
        model_type, model, experimentID, experimentDesc, condition, ratioOrder, ResponseId, measure, chance.level
    ) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
        rating = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop")

# Group level analysis
summarize_llm_exp2_descriptives <- function(dat = .){
    dat %>%
        dplyr::group_by(
            model_type, model, experimentID, experimentDesc, condition, measure, chance.level
        ) %>%
        dplyr::summarise(
            M = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
            SE = se(rating),
            p = wilcox.p(rating - chance.level),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
        dplyr::mutate(
            favoring =
                dplyr::case_when(
                    (M > chance.level) & (p <= .05) ~ "Ratios",
                    (M < chance.level) & (p <= .05) & (parse_exp_id(experimentID)$expID_clean == "exp2ac") ~ "Utility",
                    (M < chance.level) & (p <= .05) & (parse_exp_id(experimentID)$expID_clean == "exp2b") ~ "Harm",
                    TRUE ~ NA_character_
                )
        )
}

# Separately for each option order, and for both orders combined
dat_llm_results_exp2_descriptives <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    dat_llm_results_exp2_by_subject %>%
        dplyr::filter(ratioOrder == "high_ratio_first") %>%
        summarize_llm_exp2_descriptives() %>%
        dplyr::mutate(option_order = "high-ratio option first"),
    dat_llm_results_exp2_by_subject %>%
        dplyr::filter(ratioOrder == "high_ratio_second") %>%
        summarize_llm_exp2_descriptives() %>%
        dplyr::mutate(option_order = "high-ratio option second"),
    dat_llm_results_exp2_by_subject %>%
        summarize_llm_exp2_descriptives() %>%
        dplyr::mutate(option_order = "both orders")
) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        option_order = factor(
            option_order,
            levels = c("both orders", "high-ratio option first", "high-ratio option second")
        ),
        model = relabel_models(model),
        condition = relabel_conds_llm(condition)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::relocate(option_order)


dat_llm_results_exp2_descriptives_summary <-
    dat_llm_results_exp2_descriptives %>%
    dplyr::count(option_order, model_type, experimentID, condition, measure, favoring) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = favoring,
                       values_from = n) %>%
    dplyr::rename(dplyr::any_of(c("Neither" = "NA"))) %>%
    # Make sure that all columns exist, even if no model favors, e.g., harm (missing columns are added as NA)
    dplyr::bind_rows(
        tibble::tibble(Ratios = integer(), Utility = integer(), Harm = integer(), Neither = integer())
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        dplyr::across(c(Ratios, Neither), ~tidyr::replace_na(.x, 0)),
        Utility = dplyr::if_else(parse_exp_id(experimentID)$expID_clean == "exp2ac",
                              tidyr::replace_na(Utility, 0),
                              Utility),
        Harm = dplyr::if_else(parse_exp_id(experimentID)$expID_clean == "exp2b",
                              tidyr::replace_na(Harm, 0),
                              Harm)
    )
```

```{r llm-exp3-order-effects-calculate}
# Effects of the option order (ratioOrder: high-ratio option presented first or second) on the preference for the
# high-ratio option, separately for each experiment and model (including humans).
# Dependent variable: raw ratings (1-6; high values favour the high-ratio option), linear mixed models.
# Sum coding for condition (moral vs. economic) and ratioOrder. For the LLMs, condition and ratioOrder are between
# simulated participants; for humans, condition is within participants and ratioOrder between participants.
fit_llm_exp3_order_effect_model <- function(dat = .){
    lme4::lmer(
        rating ~ condition * ratioOrder +
            (1 | ResponseId) + (1 | scenario),
        data = dat
    ) %>%
        extract.results.from.model() %>%
        tibble::rownames_to_column("Effect")
}

# Condition effect separately for each option order
fit_llm_exp3_condition_effect_model <- function(dat = .){
    lme4::lmer(
        rating ~ condition +
            (1 | ResponseId) + (1 | scenario),
        data = dat
    ) %>%
        extract.results.from.model() %>%
        tibble::rownames_to_column("Effect")
}

# Data for both kinds of models
dat_llm_exp3_for_order_models <- dat_llm_results_exps_long %>%
    select_exps(
        expID_clean = c("exp2ac", "exp2b"),
        require_single_version = TRUE,
        scenarios_excluded = FALSE
    ) %>%
    dplyr::filter(measure == "raw") %>%
    classify_models() %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        # Scenario: title in the LLM data, scenarioID in the human data
        scenario = dplyr::coalesce(title, as.character(scenarioID)),
        condition = factor(condition, levels = c("moral", "economic")),
        ratioOrder = factor(ratioOrder, levels = c("high_ratio_first", "high_ratio_second"))
    )

dat_llm_exp3_order_effects <- dat_llm_exp3_for_order_models %>%
    dplyr::group_by(model_type, model, experimentID) %>%
    dplyr::group_modify(
        \(dat, dat_grp) {
            contrasts(dat$condition) <- contr.sum(2)
            contrasts(dat$ratioOrder) <- contr.sum(2)
            # Models that cannot be fitted (e.g., constant ratings) are reported as missing
            purrr::possibly(
                fit_llm_exp3_order_effect_model,
                otherwise = tibble::tibble(Effect = NA_character_)
            )(dat)
        }
    ) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup()

dat_llm_exp3_condition_effects_by_order <- dat_llm_exp3_for_order_models %>%
    dplyr::group_by(model_type, model, experimentID, ratioOrder) %>%
    dplyr::group_modify(
        \(dat, dat_grp) {
            contrasts(dat$condition) <- contr.sum(2)
            # Models that cannot be fitted (e.g., constant ratings) are reported as missing
            purrr::possibly(
                fit_llm_exp3_condition_effect_model,
                otherwise = tibble::tibble(Effect = NA_character_)
            )(dat)
        }
    ) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup()
```

# One row per model: estimate [95% CI] and p for each effect; rows grouped by experiment
dat_llm_exp3_order_effects %>%
    dplyr::filter(Effect != "(Intercept)") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        Effect = dplyr::recode(
            Effect,
            condition1 = "condition",
            ratioOrder1 = "order",
            `condition1:ratioOrder1` = "interaction"
        ),
        # No "-0.00" for values that round to 0
        estimate_ci = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", Estimate, ci.lower, ci.upper) %>%
            stringr::str_replace_all("-0\\.00(?![0-9])", "0.00"),
        p = dplyr::if_else(p < .001, "$<$.001", sprintf("%.3f", p)),
        model = relabel_models(model)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(experimentID, model, Effect, estimate_ci, p) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
        names_from = Effect,
        values_from = c(estimate_ci, p),
        names_vary = "slowest"
    ) %>%
    format_exp_info() %>%
    dplyr::arrange(experimentID, model) %>%
    dplyr::select(experimentID, model,
                  estimate_ci_condition, p_condition,
                  estimate_ci_order, p_order,
                  estimate_ci_interaction, p_interaction) %>%
    kable.packed(
        "experimentID",
        caption = "Effects of condition (moral vs. economic), option order (high-ratio option presented first vs. second) and their interaction on the preference for the high-ratio option (raw ratings, 1-6), separately for each experiment and model. Linear mixed models with random intercepts for (simulated) participants and scenarios. Estimates [95\\% CI] use sum coding, i.e., they are half the difference between the levels; positive estimates indicate a stronger preference for the high-ratio option in moral than in economic dilemmas (condition), and when the high-ratio option was presented first (order). For the LLMs, condition and option order are between simulated participants; for humans, condition is within participants.",
        col.names = c("Model", "Estimate [95\\% CI]", "$p$", "Estimate [95\\% CI]", "$p$", "Estimate [95\\% CI]", "$p$"),
        booktabs = TRUE,
        longtable = TRUE,
        escape = FALSE) %>%
    kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Condition" = 2, "Option order" = 2, "Condition x option order" = 2)) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped",
        "hold_position",
        "repeat_header"),
        font_size = 7) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_classic_2()

The results from the LLM simulations are shown in Figures \ref{fig:plot-llm-results-exp2-forest} and \ref{fig:plot-llm-exp3-moral-economic} (see Table \ref{tab:print-exp2-descriptives-print-details} for detailed results). In Experiment 3a (where we pitted Weber ratios against harm), the frontier models reproduced the human pattern. Like humans, they preferred the option with the higher *beneficiary:victim* ratio over the option with the lower harm in both moral and economic situations, and they did so irrespective of the order of the options (with the exception of Mistral Medium 3.5, which preferred the high-ratio option only when it was presented as the second option; Table \ref{tab:print-exp2-descriptives-print-details}). However, while humans preferred the high-ratio option even more in economic than in moral situations, many models did not reproduce this increase (DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6 luna at all reasoning levels, Qwen3.7-plus with reasoning) or even showed a slightly increased ratio preference in the moral condition (Gemini 3.8 Flash at all reasoning levels, Qwen3.7-plus without reasoning; Table \ref{tab:llm-exp3-order-effects-print}). 

In Experiment 3b (where we pitted Weber ratios against utility), humans preferred the high-ratio option in moral situations, but the high-utility option in economic situations. This difference between moral and economic situations was found in both option orders (Table \ref{tab:llm-exp3-condition-effects-by-order-print}). Only one model, Qwen3.7-plus with reasoning, reproduced this pattern. It preferred utility in economic situations and the high-ratio option in moral situations. The difference between moral and economic situations was reliable in both option orders. (When the high-ratio option was presented first, its preference for utility in economic situations was only marginally significant, *p* = .051.) Without reasoning, Qwen3.7-plus preferred utility in both moral and economic situations.

None of the other models reproduced the human pattern, although some models showed a greater ratio preference in the moral than in the economic condition (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6 luna at all reasoning levels; Table \ref{tab:llm-exp3-condition-effects-by-order-print}), even though this tendency was only marginal or not significant in some option orders. To the extent that the frontier models showed preferences that were consistent across the option orders, they preferred utility over *beneficiary:victim* ratios in both moral and economic situations (e.g., GPT-6 luna and Gemini 3.8 Flash at all reasoning levels, Qwen3.7-plus without reasoning, though the latter results were marginal when the high-ratio option was presented second); no frontier model consistently preferred the high-ratio option in both option orders (Table \ref{tab:print-exp2-descriptives-print-details} and Figure \ref{fig:plot-llm-exp3-moral-economic-by-order}). The preferences of the other frontier models depended strongly on the option order.

dat_llm_claude_justifications <- dat_llm_results_exp3_rerun_text_responses %>%
    # Probably not necessary
    select_exps(
        #expID_clean = c("exp2ac", "exp2b"),
        expID_clean = c("exp2ac"),
        require_single_version = FALSE
    ) %>%
    dplyr::filter(
        stringr::str_detect(model, "claude")
    ) %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(
        response_raw = stringr::str_to_lower(response_raw),
        mentions_utility = stringr::str_detect(response_raw, "\\bnets*\\b"),
        mentions_harm = stringr::str_detect(response_raw, "\\bharm\\b"),
        mentions_ratio = stringr::str_detect(response_raw, "\\bratio\\b"),
    ) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(
        dplyr::starts_with("mentions"),
        names_to = "term", 
        names_prefix = "mentions_",
        values_to = "mentioned"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::count(condition, term, mentioned) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        prop = 100 * n / sum(n),
        # Number of justifications (the same for every term)
        n_justifications = sum(n),
        .by = c(condition, term)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::filter(mentioned) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
        id_cols = c(condition, n_justifications),
        names_from = term,
        values_from = prop
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(condition = relabel_conds_llm(condition)) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(condition) %>%
    dplyr::select(condition, n_justifications, utility, ratio, harm)

```{r claude-justifications-print, eval = FALSE}
dat_llm_claude_justifications %>%
    knitr::kable(
        caption = "Justifications volunteered by Claude Sonnet 5.5 in Experiment 3b (ratio vs. utility; all reasoning efforts): number of responses containing text, and percentage of these responses mentioning the net gain (\\emph{net}), ratios (\\emph{ratio}) and harm (\\emph{harm}).",
        col.names = c("Condition", "N", "Net gain (\\%)", "Ratio (\\%)", "Harm (\\%)"),
        digits = 1,
        booktabs = TRUE,
        escape = FALSE) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped",
        "hold_position")) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_classic_2()
```

Although Claude Sonnet 5.5 was asked to respond with a single number, it often volunteered a justification for its choice in Experiment 3b. We took advantage of these unrequested justifications to examine what Claude spontaneously reasoned about. Claude almost always referred to the net gain of the two options (in `r round(min(dat_llm_claude_justifications$utility), 1)`% to `r round(max(dat_llm_claude_justifications$utility), 1)`% of these responses), and mentioned ratios in `r round(min(dat_llm_claude_justifications$ratio))`% to `r round(max(dat_llm_claude_justifications$ratio))`% of them. In contrast, the word *harm* appeared in only `r round(min(dat_llm_claude_justifications$harm), 1)`% to `r round(max(dat_llm_claude_justifications$harm), 1)`% of these responses (although Claude often referred to the number of lives or resources lost). However, even though Claude systematically computed utility, it tended to decide against maximizing utility and, on average, favored the high-ratio option in both conditions of Experiment 3b, although this preference depended considerably on the order of the options. It should be noted that these justifications are not a random sample of Claude's decisions, as they mostly occurred early in the conversations and when Claude appeared to be torn between the options.

These results are somewhat surprising, as, to our knowledge, no normative theory of moral or economic decision making prescribes decisions based on ratios. Nevertheless, Claude frequently treated ratios as a relevant consideration, suggesting that it acquired, either from its training data or from post-training alignment, the notion that ratios are relevant for decision making. This might reflect ratio-based reasoning in some of the real-world data it was trained on, although we cannot rule out that it reflects research on ratio effects in decision making (including, possibly, earlier versions of the present work). 

`r clearpage()`

Points show mean preference ratings with 95\\% confidence intervals. Humans are shown as larger diamonds. Colour indicates the significantly favoured option (blue = ratio, red = alternative, grey = no significant preference)."}

l_exp2_forest$both_orders$local

```


When considering (smaller) local LLMs, their responses were mostly based on the order of the options, with no consistent difference between moral and economic situations.


#### Summary


In Experiment 3, most models showed qualitatively different behaviors from humans. Though the frontier models reproduced the human preference for *beneficiary:victim* ratios over harm in Experiment 3a, one model (Mistral Medium 3.5) showed this preference only in one option order, and many models did not reproduce the greater preference for ratios in the economic condition. 

In Experiment 3b, with the exception of Qwen3.7-plus with reasoning, no model reproduced the human pattern, where humans preferred *beneficiary:victim* ratios over utility in moral situations, but utility over ratios in economic situations. To the extent that the frontier models showed preferences that were consistent across the option orders, they preferred utility in both moral and economic situations. Further, even Qwen3.7-plus with reasoning failed to reproduce the increased preference for ratios in the economic condition of Experiment 3a.

In both experiments, the local models mainly showed effects of the order of the options.


`r clearpage()`

### Experiment 6

Experiment 6 assessed how acceptability ratings depend on *beneficiary:victim* ratios when the deaths of the victims and the beneficiaries are equally salient vs. when the deaths of the victims are made more vivid and salient. Our critical measure is the risk ratio comparing acceptability rates when the deaths of the victims are vividly portrayed versus when they are presented with the same neutral language as the beneficiaries, $\RR = \frac{P_{\text{acceptable, vivid}}}{P_{\text{acceptable, neutral}}}$. In humans, this risk ratio is positively correlated with the *beneficiary:victim* Weber ratio, suggesting that the effect of victim salience decreases for higher Weber ratios. 


```{r relative-risk-calculate-exp11-llm}

l_llm_results_exp11_wide <- purrr::map(
    c("cloud", "local") %>% purrr::set_names(.),
    \(mdl_type){
        
        v_allowed_models <- c(
            LLM_LABELS_TIBBLE %>%
                dplyr::filter(model_type == mdl_type) %>%
                dplyr::pull(model),
            "participants"
        )

        dat_llm_results_exps %>%
            dplyr::filter(experimentID == "exp11",
                          #!str_detect(model, "claude"),
                          #model != "participants"
                          model %in% v_allowed_models
                          ) %>% 
            # Make this a pseudo within subject exp
            dplyr::mutate(ResponseId = stringr::str_remove(ResponseId, "(neutral|vivid)_")) %>%
            dplyr::select(-dplyr::matches("question|anchor|prompt|combo|text|scenarioID")) %>% 
            tidyr::pivot_wider(
                names_from = condition,
                values_from = dplyr::starts_with("rating"),
                names_vary = "slowest",
                names_glue = "{condition}_{.value}") %>% 
            dplyr::rename_with(~ str_remove(.x, "rating."), dplyr::matches("_rating")) %>% 
            make_rr_neutral_vivid(neutral_col = neutral_raw, vivid_col = vivid_raw, rr_col = RR_raw) %>% 
            make_rr_neutral_vivid(neutral_col = neutral_bin, vivid_col = vivid_bin, rr_col = RR_bin)
    }
)
        
        

```

dat_llm_results_exp11_wide_correlations <- l_llm_results_exp11_wide %>%

    tidyr::pivot_longer(
        cols = dplyr::starts_with("RR"),

    dplyr::group_by(experimentID, model_type, model, measure) %>%

#### Summary 
Overall, these results suggest that the models generally reproduced the correlation between the risk ratio and the Weber ratio, though the quantitative fit is of variable quality.


## Overall Summary

The frontier LLMs showed several key similarities to human moral judgment. Most models demonstrated sensitivity to *beneficiary:victim* Weber ratios, greater acceptance of sacrifices in economic versus moral decisions, and a decreasing effect of victim salience at higher Weber ratios. However, the quantitative fit to the psychophysical model varied considerably across models, and some models failed to show expected patterns.

These similarities appeared to depend on model size and presumably on massive amounts of training data (or on differences in alignment processes), as the smaller local models largely failed to reproduce human behavior. Local models showed no discernible sensitivity to Weber ratios in Experiment 2 and exhibited inconsistent patterns across other experiments.

However, with the exception of Qwen3.7-plus with reasoning, all models behaved qualitatively differently from humans in Experiment 3b. To the extent that the other models showed a consistent preference, they preferred utility over ratios in both moral and economic conditions. Further, even Qwen3.7-plus with reasoning reproduced the results of Experiment 3a only partially.
